current_job: Line cook at a restaurant
headline: From the jail kitchen to running a line
journey: Inside, I ran the breakfast line for about 180 people every morning. Up at 4, eggs, oatmeal, trays out by 6. I did that for three years. When I got out, I honestly didn't think any of it counted. I put 'none' under work history on my first application. Then I started applying for real, and it was rough. I filled out something like 40 applications. Two places offered me a job and then took it back after the background check. One manager told me to my face I'd be a risk. I cried in my car, which was really my cousin's car. A county culinary training program changed things. It was 10 weeks, and the instructor made us write down every single thing we did in a kitchen, inside or out. That list became my resume. She also practiced interviews with me until I could talk about my gap without my voice shaking. It still took me four months to get hired. I started as a prep cook at a restaurant downtown, chopping onions for hours. Eight months later they moved me to the line. Now I make about $22 an hour, and I train the new cooks. Some of them came from where I came from.
advice: Rejections are not the final answer. I got told no for four months straight. Keep a list of where you applied, keep going, and write down everything you did in that kitchen.

current_job: Kitchen supervisor at a hospital cafeteria
headline: From kitchen crew to kitchen supervisor
journey: I worked the jail kitchen for three years. Meal prep, safe food handling, cleaning the walk-in, keeping count of every knife. When I came home, my daughter was nine and I needed a paycheck fast. I didn't know how to talk about what I did inside, so I just didn't. That was a mistake. A woman at a reentry center sat with me and helped me write it down plainly: prepped meals for 300 people, followed food safety rules, trained new crew. Seeing it on paper made me sit up straighter. I got my Food Handler card in one day and landed a prep cook job at a cafe. About $18 an hour. Childcare was the hard part. My mom watched my daughter, but only until 3, so I begged for morning shifts. After eight months I moved to line cook at a busier place and stayed two years. Then I did a 12-week culinary training on my days off. That's where I learned costing, ordering, and scheduling. Now I supervise a kitchen at a hospital in San Jose. I run a team of 11 and make about $27 an hour. I still get to work the line when we're short, which I love.
advice: Start with what you already know, then ask what you need next. Your kitchen time inside is real experience. Say it plainly.

current_job: Certified nursing assistant at a care home
headline: From cleaning crew to nursing assistant
journey: Inside, I was on the cleaning crew for a year. Floors, bathrooms, the medical unit. I liked the medical unit best. I was careful, and the nurses noticed. One of them told me I should be a CNA. When I got out, I wanted to sign up for CNA classes right away. But a friend of mine had paid $1,200 for a program and then found out she couldn't get certified. So I did something different. I called the state licensing office first. It took three calls and a lot of hold music. They explained the process, what they look at, and what papers I'd need. That one step saved me so much worry. While I waited, I worked as a janitor at an office building for a year, about $18 an hour. I took two buses each way, 70 minutes, with my son's daycare in the middle. I studied flash cards on the bus. Then I did a 12-week CNA program that works with people with records. Now I work at a care home in Hayward. I help residents bathe, eat, and move safely. I make about $22 an hour. One resident calls me 'the careful one.' I'll take it.
advice: Call the licensing board before you sign up for anything. Knowing your options first means you don't waste money or hope.

current_job: Sterile processing tech at a hospital
headline: Laundry inside taught me to never skip a step
journey: I ran the big washers in laundry for almost four years inside. Sorting, temperatures, chemicals, logging every load. It was hot and boring, but I got very good at following a checklist exactly. I also finished my GED in there at 38. My teacher cried more than I did. After I came home, I worked nights stocking shelves and felt stuck. Then a counselor at a job center asked if I'd ever heard of sterile processing. I hadn't. It's the people who clean, check, and pack surgical tools so they're safe for the next surgery. She said, 'You already know how to follow a strict process.' She was right. The hard part was the computer. The training had online quizzes and I had never really used email. My niece taught me on her laptop at the kitchen table, two nights a week. I passed the program and then the certification exam on my second try. My first hospital said no after the background check. The second one said yes. Now I've been at a hospital in San Francisco for three years. I make about $29 an hour. Every tray I send up, I know exactly what's on it.
advice: If you were good at a boring job inside, that's a skill. Hospitals need people who don't skip steps. Learn email early, it matters more than you think.
recent_activity: Commented on a post about hospital jobs
personality: Quiet, precise, a little dry. Explains things in order, step one, step two. Warms up once she trusts you.
voice_sample: Nobody knew what sterile processing was when I started either. It's the job behind the surgery. You'd be surprised how much you already know.
intro_message: Hi. Lorena here. I work in sterile processing at a hospital. Not a lot of people know about it. Want me to explain what it's like?
boundaries: Doesn't talk about her case or family. Not a formal mentor yet, but happy to answer questions about the job.

current_job: Home health aide with a home care agency
headline: I was a caregiver my whole life before it was my job
journey: I raised four kids and took care of my mother when she got sick. I also watched neighbors' kids for cash for years. Nobody called that work, but it was. When I came home at 51, I had no resume and no ID. My license had expired and my birth certificate was lost. Getting a state ID took me six weeks and three trips to the DMV on the bus. A volunteer at a church helped me order my birth certificate and paid the fee. I'll never forget that. A reentry program connected me with home care training. Two weeks of classes, CPR, and a background check. I was so nervous about that check. The agency told me some things matter for this kind of work and some don't, and they walked me through it. I got cleared. Now I visit three clients a week. I help them shower, cook, take their pills on time, and get to the doctor. One of my ladies is 92 and tells me stories about dancing in the 1950s. I make about $20 an hour. I still don't drive, so I plan my bus routes every Sunday night with a highlighter.
advice: Get your ID first. Everything else waits on that. And if you raised kids or cared for family, you have caregiving experience. Say so.

current_job: Assistant teacher at a childcare center
headline: My GED inside led me to a classroom full of toddlers
journey: I was 22 when I went in, and I didn't have my diploma. I got my GED inside, plus a few college units in child development through a program that came in twice a week. I loved it, but honestly, I figured nobody would ever let me work with kids. When I got out, I moved in with my auntie and my two boys. I needed hours that ended by 4 so I could pick them up. Most jobs I found were nights or weekends. I worked at a car wash for cash for a while. Then a counselor at the community college told me my child development units still counted. I took two more classes, 12 units total. Getting fingerprinted for childcare work scared me to death. I asked the counselor to explain the clearance process before I applied anywhere. Turns out it depends a lot on the details, and some people do get cleared. I did. Now I'm an assistant teacher in the toddler room at a center in Richmond. I make about $19 an hour, and my hours are 7:30 to 3:30, which is perfect. My boys go to school right down the street.
advice: Ask how the clearance works before you give up on a field. Don't assume the answer is no. And look for jobs that match your kids' schedule.

current_job: Crew lead, commercial cleaning
headline: A cleaning job gave me a paycheck and a reference
journey: Inside I was on the janitorial crew. I mopped the same hallway every day for two years. Sounds small, but I learned which chemicals don't mix, how to use a floor machine, and how to finish on time. When I got out, I just needed a paycheck, any paycheck. My parole officer gave me a list of places that hire people with records. A commercial cleaning company was on it. They hired me for nights, cleaning office buildings, about $17 an hour. I showed up early every single night. Not once late in the first year. That was on purpose. I knew I needed a good reference more than anything. The hard part was the schedule. Working 10 at night to 6 in the morning messed up my sleep and my mood. I almost quit twice. My sister kept telling me, one more month. After 14 months, my supervisor made me a crew lead. Now I run a crew of six across three buildings. I do the schedule, train new people, and handle the client walk-throughs. I make about $23 an hour. When someone new starts and they're nervous, I tell them I started the same way.
advice: Your first steady job is about building a reference. Show up early, every time. That reference opens the next door.

current_job: Housekeeping supervisor at a hotel
headline: I cleaned houses for cash for 15 years. Now I run a hotel floor
journey: Before everything, I cleaned houses for cash. Fifteen years, maybe eight houses a week. I was fast and people trusted me with their keys. But I never had a pay stub, so on paper I had no work history at all. When I came home, that was the first wall I hit. Applications asked for past employers and phone numbers. I had none. A job coach at a reentry program told me to ask two of my old house clients for letters. I was embarrassed, but I did it. Both said yes. One wrote a full page. I took those letters to a hotel job fair. They hired me as a room attendant, about $24 an hour with the union. Sixteen rooms a day. My back hurt for the first month. I took the bus and the train, an hour each way, and left the house at 5:15. After two years, the head of housekeeping asked me to train new people because I was fast and careful. Then I became a supervisor. Now I check rooms, plan the daily board, and handle guest complaints. I speak Spanish and English, which helps a lot with my team.
advice: Cash work is still work. Ask the people you worked for to write a letter. It's not begging. It's proof.

current_job: Licensed cosmetologist at a salon
headline: I did hair in my unit. Now I have my own chair
journey: I've been doing hair since I was 12. Braids, presses, everything. Inside, I did hair for half my unit with whatever we had, which was not much. Then I got into the cosmetology program there and started logging real hours. I had almost 1,000 hours when I came home. The big question was whether I could even get licensed with a record. Everyone had a different opinion. I stopped listening to rumors and contacted the state board myself. I also found a free legal clinic that helped me put together my paperwork: letters, my certificate, proof of the program. It took about five months to hear back. Those months were hard. I braided hair in my kitchen for cash and kept a notebook of every client. Then I finished my remaining hours at a beauty school in Oakland and passed both parts of the exam. My first salon job was shampoo and assisting, about $16 an hour plus tips. Now I rent a chair, and I'm booked four days a week. I specialize in natural hair and protective styles. I still keep that notebook. It has 300 names in it now.
advice: Don't listen to rumors about licensing. Ask the board yourself and get help with the paperwork. Then keep practicing while you wait.

current_job: Nail technician at a nail salon
headline: Nails at the kitchen table to a licensed tech
journey: My aunt has done nails for 25 years. I grew up sweeping her salon and painting my cousins' nails at the kitchen table. Before I went in, I helped at her shop for cash, but I never got my license. When I came home, I had a daughter in first grade and I had check-ins in the mornings twice a month. I needed a job that was flexible and done by 5. Nail salons can be flexible, but you need the license. I didn't know if I could get one. My aunt's friend, who teaches at a beauty school, told me to apply and be honest. The school had a payment plan, $150 a month. I went to classes from 9 to 2 while my daughter was in school. 400 hours took me about five months. The exam was the scary part. The written test was in English and I read slower, so I practiced with an app every night after my daughter slept. I passed on the first try. Now I work at a salon in San Jose, Tuesday to Saturday, 10 to 5. I make about $18 an hour plus tips. My specialty is gel and nail art. Regulars ask for me by name.

current_job: Shift lead at a discount store
headline: My first real job ever, at 24. Now I'm a shift lead
journey: I'd never had a real job before. Not one. I went in at 19, and before that I was just trying to survive. When I came home at 23, every application asked for work history and I had nothing to put. I felt so behind everyone. A program for young women coming home helped me make a resume that started with skills instead of jobs. Things like counting commissary, keeping my area clean, and helping other girls write letters. It sounded silly to me, but it worked. I applied to 22 stores. I got three interviews. In the first two, I froze when they asked about the gap. So my coach and I practiced a short answer, three sentences, until I could say it without crying. At the third interview, I said it, and the manager just nodded and asked when I could start. I started as a cashier at about $17 an hour. I took the bus, 40 minutes, and I was never late. After a year they made me a shift lead. Now I count the drawers, open the store, and train new cashiers. I'm 24. It's my first real job and I'm good at it.
advice: Practice your answer about the gap out loud until it's boring. Three sentences. Then stop talking and let them ask the next question.

current_job: Customer service rep for a utility company
headline: I learned computers at 44 and now I answer 60 calls a day
journey: Inside, I worked as a clerk in the education office. I filed papers, answered the phone, and kept the sign-in sheets. It was the first time anyone told me I was organized. But we used old computers, and when I came home, everything was different. Phones, online applications, passwords. I didn't even have an email. I went to the library in Richmond three mornings a week for a free computer class. The teacher was patient. I learned typing, email, and how to fill out applications online. I went from 15 words a minute to 40. I needed daytime hours because I was caring for my grandson after school. A workforce program had a customer service training, six weeks, with mock calls. I was terrible at first. I talked too fast. They recorded me and played it back, which was so embarrassing, but it helped. The program connected me to a call center job at a utility company. About $23 an hour, 7 to 3:30, with benefits. I take about 60 calls a day: billing, payment plans, outages. Some people yell. I let them, and then I help them. Last month my supervisor asked me to sit with new hires.
advice: Go to the library. The computer classes are free and nobody judges you. Learn email first, then typing. It opens everything.

current_job: Front desk receptionist at a health clinic
headline: The library clerk inside became the friendly face at the front desk
journey: I worked in the library inside for five years. Checking books in and out, keeping records, helping women find what they needed. I also earned a certificate in office skills through a program that came in. Word, Excel, filing, phone manners. I was proud of that certificate, but I worried it wouldn't mean anything outside. When I came home at 52, I stayed in a transitional house for eight months. That gave me a stable address, which turned out to matter a lot for applications. I applied for front desk jobs and heard nothing. Twenty applications, zero calls. A job developer looked at my resume and said I was hiding my best stuff. I'd left off the library job and the certificate because I was ashamed of where I got them. She helped me write them as plain experience. The calls started coming. A community health clinic in Oakland hired me. They told me they liked that I had lived experience. Now I check in about 80 patients a day, schedule appointments, and handle insurance cards. I make about $24 an hour. Patients who are nervous come to my desk first, and I can tell when someone needs a minute.
advice: Don't hide experience because of where you got it. A certificate is a certificate. Put it on the paper and let them see it.

current_job: Bookkeeping clerk at a property management office
headline: College credits inside turned into a desk job with numbers
journey: I was always good at math, but nobody ever pushed me. Inside, I took college classes through a program that came in. I earned 24 credits, including accounting and business math. That felt good, all of us studying together. Then I found a part-time bookkeeping job at a small property management office. Twenty hours a week, about $21 an hour. After four months they made it full time. Now I enter rent payments, pay vendors, and do the monthly reports. My boss says I catch mistakes nobody else sees.

current_job: Construction laborer on commercial job sites
headline: Fire crew made me strong. Now I build things
journey: I spent two seasons on a fire crew. We cut fire line with hand tools, 12 to 16 hours a day, carrying 45 pounds up hills. I was the smallest one on my crew and I kept up. That changed how I saw myself. When I came home, I wanted to keep working with my body, not sit at a desk. But I didn't have a car, and most construction jobs start at 6 in the morning, way out of town. A pre-apprenticeship program in Oakland was the answer. Twelve weeks of tool safety, math, blueprint reading, and getting my OSHA 10 card. They also helped me buy steel-toe boots and gave me a bus pass. The math part was hard. I hadn't done fractions since middle school. I stayed after class with a tutor twice a week. After graduation, I got placed as a laborer through the union hall. About $28 an hour. I carry materials, set up and clean the site, and help the carpenters. I take BART and a bus, and I'm out the door at 4:45. I'm saving for a car and studying for the carpentry apprenticeship test.
advice: Do a pre-apprenticeship. They help with boots, tools, bus passes, and the math. And if you did fire crew, you already know hard work.

current_job: Electrician apprentice, third year
headline: I wired my first outlet inside. Now I'm halfway to journeyman
journey: Inside, I took an electrical class through the vocational program. I wired my first outlet at 29 and got hooked. I earned a pre-apprenticeship certificate before I came home. When I got out, I thought the union would take me right away. They didn't. The apprenticeship has an aptitude test with algebra and reading, and I failed it the first time by a few points. That hurt. I was the only woman in the waiting room that day. My voice shook, but I told them about the outlet, the class, and how I had taught two other women in my unit. I got in. The first year was hard. Lots of digging, carrying conduit, and some guys who didn't want me there. A woman journeyman took me under her wing, and that changed everything. Now I'm in my third year. I make about $40 an hour, and it goes up every six months. I go to class two nights a week.
advice: If you fail the test, take it again. I did. Study the algebra a little every day, and find one woman in the trade to lean on.

current_job: Maintenance technician at an apartment complex

current_job: Forklift lead at a distribution warehouse
headline: From laundry crew to forklift lead
journey: I worked in laundry inside for three years, then ran the supply room. Sorting, counting, tracking what came in and went out, keeping a busy team organized. I didn't know it then, but that's warehouse work. When I came home, a friend told me warehouses hire fast and don't always care about your past. Some do, some don't. I applied to six through a temp agency. Two turned me down after the background check. The third hired me as a picker on nights, about $19 an hour. I walked about 10 miles a shift. My feet were wrecked for a month. Good shoes are worth every dollar. After three months, the company paid for my forklift certification. It was one day of training and a driving test. I was nervous, but I passed. Driving the forklift felt like flying after all that walking. I kept my numbers high and never missed a shift. After a year, they made me forklift lead. Now I train new drivers, plan where loads go, and do the safety checks every morning. I make about $25 an hour. I also switched to days, which my body thanks me for.
advice: Ask if the warehouse will pay for your forklift certification. Many do after a few months. Buy good shoes before your first shift.

current_job: Delivery driver for a parcel service
headline: Getting my license back was the whole job search
journey: Before I went in, I never had a job on paper. I was a teen mom and my grandma helped raise my son. When I came home at 25, I had no ID, a suspended license, and no clue where to start. Every good job I saw near Vallejo needed a car or a license. So my real job search started at the DMV. A legal aid clinic helped me figure out the fines and fees on my license. Some got reduced, and I got on a payment plan for the rest. That took about four months and a lot of paperwork. I got my state ID first, then my license back. I cried in the DMV parking lot. While I waited, I did a short warehouse job through a temp agency, packing boxes, about $18 an hour. My grandma watched my son. Once I had my license, I applied to drive delivery vans. They checked my driving record, not just my background. I got hired. Now I deliver about 150 packages a day around Vallejo and Benicia. I make about $23 an hour. I like being alone in the van with my music. I'm home by 6 for dinner with my son.
advice: Get help with your license fines before you give up on driving jobs. Legal aid helped me for free. Your ID and license open a lot of doors.

current_job: Seasonal wildland firefighter
headline: I fought fires on a crew inside. Now I do it for a paycheck
journey: I spent three seasons on a fire crew while I was inside. Cutting line, mopping up hot spots, sleeping in the dirt. I earned my basic wildland firefighter certificates there, plus first aid and CPR. My crew boss said I was the steadiest person he had. When I came home, I wanted to keep fighting fire, but I didn't know if anyone would hire me. I'd heard California passed a law that could help people with fire crew experience clear their records. I found a free legal clinic, and they walked me through the process. It took about seven months. In the meantime, I worked at a gym front desk and ran every morning to stay in shape. Then I found a fire training center that works with women who served on crews. They helped me get my certificates updated and my physical fitness test ready. I applied to a seasonal hand crew. I passed the pack test, three miles with 45 pounds in under 45 minutes. Now I've done two seasons. I make about $24 an hour plus lots of overtime in summer. In the off-season I take EMT classes at the community college.
advice: If you were on fire crew, look into getting your record cleared. Ask a free legal clinic. Keep training while you wait, the pack test is no joke.

current_job: Crew lead, fire prevention and brush clearing
headline: Clearing brush so fires don't start. And leading the crew
journey: I did two seasons on a fire crew inside. It was the hardest work of my life and the first time I felt part of a real team. When I came home, I had three kids to get back. Full-time fire season, away from home for weeks, just wasn't possible for me. I had to find a way to use those skills and still sleep in my own bed. A friend from my old crew told me about fire prevention work. Clearing brush, cutting fire breaks, and thinning trees around neighborhoods before fire season. Same tools, same safety rules, but you're home most nights. I got hired on a crew with a land management group in the hills near San Jose. About $22 an hour to start. My chainsaw skills were rusty, so I took a weekend saw class. After a year, I became the crew lead. Now I run eight people. I plan the work, check the gear, and make sure everybody drinks water and goes home safe. Half of my crew came from fire crews too. I make about $28 an hour now. I get home by 5, help with homework, and fall asleep on the couch.
advice: Fire crew skills work in more than one job. If you can't leave your kids for weeks, look at fire prevention and brush clearing. Same skills, home at night.

current_job: Community health worker at a neighborhood clinic
headline: Walking beside people, because someone walked beside me
journey: I'm 63, and I've been in recovery for 11 years. I say that out loud because it's part of why I'm good at my job. Inside, I worked as a peer helper in the medical unit. I sat with women who were scared, helped them fill out forms, and reminded them about appointments. When I came home, I was 52, with no recent work history, no apartment, and not much hope. I stayed in a shelter, then a room in a shared house. A community health worker visited me, helped me get Medi-Cal, and took me to my first doctor's appointment in years. She never once rushed me. I remember thinking, I want to do that. I volunteered at a clinic for a year, then did a 16-week community health worker certificate at City College. Now I work at a neighborhood clinic in San Francisco. I help people sign up for health coverage, get to appointments, find food and housing, and understand what the doctor said. I make about $27 an hour. Some of my clients just got out. I can tell, and they can tell I know. That trust is everything.
advice: Your story can be your strength in this work. You don't have to share all of it. But the parts you share can help someone feel less alone.
skills: Connecting people to food and housing

current_job: Peer reentry specialist at a nonprofit
headline: I meet women at the gate on their first day home
journey: Inside, I was a peer mentor and a tutor in the GED class. I helped about 30 women pass their tests, and I got a peer support certificate through a program that came in. I've also been in recovery for eight years, and I'm open about that. When I came home, I had a plan on paper, but the first week fell apart. My ride didn't show up. My phone didn't work. The shelter bed I was promised was gone. A woman from a reentry nonprofit found me at the bus station with my paper bag of stuff. She bought me lunch, got me a phone, and drove me to a bed. That day is why I do this work. I volunteered with that same nonprofit for six months while I worked at a coffee shop. Then they hired me part-time, and later full-time. Now I'm a peer reentry specialist in Oakland. I meet women on their first day out, help with IDs, phones, housing lists, benefits, and job referrals. I carry about 25 women at a time. I make about $26 an hour. The best part is when someone I met on day one calls to tell me she got hired.
advice: The first week is the hardest. Have a backup plan for your ride, your phone, and your bed. And ask for help early. That's not weakness.

current_job: Medical assistant at a family clinic
headline: From the infirmary mop bucket to taking vital signs
journey: Inside, I cleaned the infirmary and helped the nurses stock supplies. I watched them take blood pressure and give shots, and I asked a hundred questions. One nurse let me practice reading the blood pressure cuff on her. When I came home, I wanted healthcare, but I was scared of the background check. Medical assisting in California doesn't need a state license, which helped. Still, some clinics check closely. I asked every school how many of their students with records got placed. One school in San Jose was honest and said, 'Most, but not all.' I liked that answer. The program was nine months, and I paid with a grant from a workforce center. I didn't have a car, so I took a bus and light rail, an hour each way, and studied medical words on my phone. My mom kept my daughter after school. My externship was at a family clinic. I worked hard, learned everyone's name, and they hired me when it ended. Now I take vital signs, room patients, give shots, and update charts. I make about $23 an hour. My daughter tells her friends I'm basically a doctor.
advice: Ask schools straight up how their students with records do getting hired. Treat your externship like a three-month job interview, because it is.

personality: Curious and earnest. Asks lots of questions back. Loves learning. Slightly nervous energy, but very kind. Mentions her daughter with pride.
